reason: The provided sources fully support a surprising 45-second story with at least 10 fully verified claims.
story: When World War I broke out in August 1914, Canadian cavalry veterinarian Lieutenant Harry Colebourn volunteered to serve. En route to a mobilization camp in Quebec, his train stopped in White River, Ontario, on August 24. There, he bought a young female black bear cub from a hunter for just twenty dollars, naming her Winnipeg, or Winnie, after his adopted hometown. Winnie became the unofficial mascot of the Canadian Army Veterinary Corps and sailed across the Atlantic with thousands of troops aboard the S.S. Manitou on October 3. When Colebourn's brigade was ordered to the trenches of France, he could not take her. He left Winnie at the London Zoo in December 1914. She became so gentle and playful that A.A. Milne's son, Christopher Robin, fell in love with her during visits, inspiring the world-famous children's literary character Winnie-the-Pooh.
angle: The real Winnie-the-Pooh was a living black bear cub bought for $20 at an ordinary Canadian train stop by a WWI cavalry vet.

claims.claim: Lieutenant Harry Colebourn purchased a black bear cub for $20 on August 24, 1914.
The purchase took place at a train stop in White River, Ontario.
Colebourn named the bear Winnie after his hometown of Winnipeg, Manitoba.
Winnie sailed to England with Canadian troops aboard the S.S. Manitou on October 3, 1914.
Winnie served as the mascot for the Canadian Army Veterinary Corps and a pet for the Second Canadian Infantry Brigade.
Colebourn left Winnie at the London Zoo on December 9, 1914, before heading to the battlefields of France.
Colebourn officially donated Winnie to the London Zoo in 1919.
Christopher Robin Milne began frequently visiting Winnie at the London Zoo starting in 1924.
Christopher Robin renamed his own teddy bear after Winnipeg Bear, inspiring his father A.A. Milne's books.
The first Winnie-the-Pooh book was published in 1926.
Winnie died at the London Zoo on May 12, 1934, at the age of 20.

disputed: The exact identity of the hunter who sold the bear and provided its early socialization is undocumented and should be omitted.

Whether Winnie was called after Pooh or Pooh after Winnie is jokingly questioned in Milne's book introduction, but historical records confirm Winnipeg came first; scripts should attribute the confusion playfully to Milne's introduction if used.
